questions.stem: Stainless steel is widely used for cutlery, surgical instruments, and kitchen equipment due to its corrosion resistance. Its primary components are iron, chromium, and:
questions.explanation: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron (Fe) with at least 10.5% chromium (Cr) and typically 8–12% nickel (Ni). Chromium forms a self-healing passive oxide layer (Cr₂O₃) that prevents rusting. The standard 18/8 stainless steel contains 18% Cr and 8% Ni. 304 and 316 grades are the most common in everyday use.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Bronze, one of the earliest known alloys used by humans (Bronze Age ~3300 BCE), is a combination of:
questions.explanation: Bronze is an alloy of copper (Cu) and tin (Sn), typically about 88% Cu and 12% Sn. Bronze is harder than pure copper and was used for tools, weapons, statues, and coins in antiquity. It should be distinguished from brass, which is Cu + Zn. 'Bell metal' is a high-tin bronze (~78% Cu + 22% Sn) used specifically for making bells.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Brass, widely used for musical instruments, taps, and decorative items, is an alloy of copper and:
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy of copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn). The ratio varies: cartridge brass is 70% Cu + 30% Zn; yellow brass is 67% Cu + 33% Zn. Higher zinc content makes it harder but less ductile. Brass is used for musical instruments (trumpets, trombones), plumbing fittings, electrical connectors, and doorknobs due to its acoustic and machinability properties.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: German Silver (also called Nickel Silver) is used in cheap silverware and musical instrument keys. Despite its name, it contains NO silver. Its actual composition is:
questions.explanation: German Silver (Nickel Silver) is an alloy of copper (60%), zinc (20–25%), and nickel (15–20%) — it contains absolutely no silver. Its silvery appearance comes from nickel. It is used for making cheap cutlery (EPNS — electroplated nickel silver), musical instrument keys, spectacle frames, and zippers. The name is misleading and a classic exam trap.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Duralumin, used extensively in aircraft construction because of its high strength-to-weight ratio, is an aluminium alloy primarily containing aluminium with:
questions.explanation: Duralumin is an aluminium alloy containing approximately Al (94%) + Cu (4%) + Mg (0.5–1%) + Mn (0.5–1%). Copper adds strength through precipitation hardening; magnesium and manganese further enhance strength and corrosion resistance. It is used in aircraft fuselages, rocket bodies, and bicycle frames. It was developed by Alfred Wilm in Germany around 1909.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Galvanization is the process of coating iron or steel with a thin layer of which metal to prevent rusting?
questions.explanation: Galvanization coats iron/steel with zinc (Zn) to prevent corrosion. Zinc protects steel through two mechanisms: (1) it forms a barrier coating, and (2) since zinc is more reactive than iron (higher in the electrochemical series), it acts as a sacrificial anode — it corrodes preferentially, protecting the underlying iron even if the coating is scratched. Tinning (tin coating) is used for food cans but offers only barrier protection.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Solder, used to join electronic components and plumbing pipes, is an alloy composed of:
questions.explanation: Traditional solder is an alloy of lead (Pb) and tin (Sn). Common compositions include 50:50 (plumber's solder), 60:40 Sn:Pb (electrical solder), and eutectic 63:37 Sn:Pb (melting point 183°C). Due to environmental concerns, lead-free solders (Sn + Cu + Ag or Sn + Ag) are now mandated by RoHS regulations in electronics. Solder has a lower melting point than the metals being joined.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Dental amalgam, still used in some fillings, is a special alloy in which mercury is mixed with which metal powder?
questions.explanation: Dental amalgam consists of approximately 50% liquid mercury mixed with a powder alloy of silver (Ag ~60%), tin (Sn ~27%), copper (Cu ~13%), and trace zinc. When mixed, it forms a plastic mass that hardens within minutes. Mercury is bound chemically in the set amalgam, making it stable. The WHO has been phasing down amalgam use over dental health and environmental mercury concerns.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Gunmetal (also called Red Brass), used for casting gears, valves, and ship fittings, has which approximate composition?
questions.explanation: Gunmetal (Red Brass) is an alloy of approximately 88% copper (Cu) + 10% tin (Sn) + 2% zinc (Zn). It was originally used for cannons (guns) because it is strong, corrosion-resistant in seawater, and does not spark when struck. It is now used for valves, pumps, gears, and marine hardware. The zinc improves fluidity for casting.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust. What percentage of the crust does aluminium constitute (approximately)?
questions.explanation: Aluminium constitutes approximately 8% of the Earth's crust by weight, making it the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element overall (after oxygen and silicon). Despite its abundance, aluminium was historically expensive because it could not easily be isolated from its ores. The Hall–Héroult process (1886) made commercial aluminium production feasible.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: An amalgam is a special category of alloy because:
options: A) It is used in aviation components
B) It contains a rare-earth metal as one component
C) One of its components is always mercury (Hg)
D) It is formed only at extremely high temperatures above 1000°C
questions.explanation: An amalgam is any alloy in which mercury (Hg) is one of the components. Mercury is liquid at room temperature (melting point −38.8°C), so amalgams are often formed by simply mixing mercury with a solid metal powder — no heat is required. Sodium amalgam is used as a reducing agent in organic chemistry; gold amalgam was historically used in gold extraction (mercury amalgamation process).
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Rose gold, popular in jewellery for its pinkish-red hue, is an alloy of gold and which metal that gives it that characteristic colour?
questions.explanation: Rose gold is an alloy of gold (Au) and copper (Cu). The higher the copper content, the redder the colour. Common 18-karat rose gold is 75% Au + 25% Cu. White gold is Au + Pd or Au + Ni. Yellow gold jewellery typically has a small amount of silver and copper added for hardness. Rose gold is also called 'Russian gold' or 'pink gold.'
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Steel is an extremely important industrial alloy. In its simplest form, steel is primarily a combination of:
questions.explanation: Steel is primarily an alloy of iron (Fe) and carbon (C), with carbon content between 0.02% and 2.1% by weight. The carbon content determines the type: low-carbon (mild) steel (<0.3%), medium-carbon (0.3–0.6%), high-carbon (>0.6%). Pure iron is too soft for structural use; carbon interstitially occupies the iron lattice, increasing strength. Other elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) are added to make specialty steels.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: High-Speed Steel (HSS), used for drill bits and cutting tools because it retains hardness at high temperatures, primarily contains iron with which key alloying element?
questions.explanation: High-Speed Steel (HSS) contains iron + typically 18% tungsten (W) + 4% chromium + 1% vanadium. Tungsten (or molybdenum as a substitute) is the primary element that gives HSS its 'red hardness' — the ability to stay hard even when cutting at temperatures where the tool glows red (~600°C). HSS is used for drill bits, milling cutters, saw blades, and lathe tools.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Bell metal, used for casting temple bells and gongs, has a higher tin content than ordinary bronze to achieve a sonorous ring. Its approximate composition is:
questions.explanation: Bell metal contains approximately 78% copper (Cu) and 22% tin (Sn) — significantly more tin than standard bronze (~12% Sn). The higher tin content gives bell metal its distinctive sonorous quality, producing a clear, long-lasting ring. Increasing tin beyond ~22% makes the metal too brittle. Church bells, temple bells, and Tibetan singing bowls are made from bell metal.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Cupronickel, widely used in circulation coins (including Indian 50-paise and older 25-paise coins), is an alloy of:
questions.explanation: Cupronickel is an alloy of copper (Cu) and nickel (Ni), with common compositions of 75% Cu + 25% Ni (as in UK 5p and 10p coins) or 80% Cu + 20% Ni. It is highly resistant to corrosion in seawater (used in marine heat exchangers), and its silvery appearance and durability make it ideal for coinage. Indian circulation coins use cupronickel and stainless steel alloys.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Nichrome, an alloy of nickel and chromium, is specifically used in which application due to its high resistivity and resistance to oxidation at high temperatures?
questions.explanation: Nichrome (Ni ~80% + Cr ~20%) is the standard material for electrical heating elements in electric coils, toasters, hair dryers, electric furnaces, and resistance wire. Its high electrical resistivity (~1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m) and ability to withstand oxidation up to 1250°C without deteriorating make it ideal. It was patented by Albert Marsh in 1905.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Monel metal, known for its exceptional resistance to corrosion in harsh environments including seawater and hydrofluoric acid, is primarily an alloy of:
questions.explanation: Monel (Monel 400) is an alloy of approximately 67% nickel (Ni) + 30% copper (Cu) + trace amounts of iron, manganese, and carbon. It was developed by Robert Crooks Stanley at INCO in 1905 and named after Ambrose Monell. Monel is used in marine propeller shafts, chemical processing equipment, and valves where resistance to corrosion by acids, alkalis, and seawater is critical.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Alnico is a widely used alloy for making permanent magnets in speakers, electric motors, and guitar pickups. Its name is derived from its component metals, which are:
questions.explanation: Alnico is a ferromagnetic alloy consisting of Al (aluminium) + Ni (nickel) + Co (cobalt) + Fe (iron), plus trace copper. The name 'Alnico' is derived from Al + Ni + Co. It was one of the first commercially useful permanent magnet materials, developed in the 1930s. Alnico magnets have high magnetic flux density and excellent temperature stability, making them ideal for guitar pickups and vintage audio equipment.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Invar (short for 'invariable') is a remarkable alloy whose volume barely changes with temperature. It is an alloy of iron and which metal (with approximately 36% of that metal)?
questions.explanation: Invar is an Fe + Ni alloy containing approximately 36% nickel, discovered by Charles Édouard Guillaume in 1896 (Nobel Prize 1920). Its coefficient of thermal expansion is nearly zero near room temperature due to magnetostrictive compensation. Invar is used in precision instruments, pendulum clocks, scientific apparatus, and LNG tank construction where dimensional stability over temperature is critical.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Type metal, historically used to cast movable type in printing presses (Gutenberg era through the 20th century), is an alloy of lead, antimony, and:
questions.explanation: Type metal is an alloy of lead (Pb ~60–80%), antimony (Sb ~15–25%), and tin (Sn ~5–10%). Lead is the base metal for low cost and low melting point; antimony expands on solidification (unlike most metals) to fill mould details sharply; tin improves fluidity and surface hardness. This combination allowed accurate casting of letter shapes. Johannes Gutenberg used type metal in his 15th-century printing press.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Wood's metal is a low-melting alloy (melting point ~70°C) used as a trigger in automatic sprinkler systems. Its four components are bismuth, lead, tin, and:
questions.explanation: Wood's metal (also called Lipowitz alloy) consists of approximately 50% bismuth (Bi) + 26.7% lead (Pb) + 13.3% tin (Sn) + 10% cadmium (Cd). Its melting point (~70°C, below the boiling point of water) makes it ideal for fire sprinkler fuse links — the sprinkler plug melts when temperature rises in a fire. Named after Barnabas Wood who patented it in 1860.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Tin cans used for food preservation are actually made of steel coated with which metal to prevent corrosion and interaction with food?
questions.explanation: Tin cans ('tin cans') are made of steel coated with a very thin layer of tin (Sn). Tin is non-toxic, corrosion-resistant, and does not react with most food acids. The coating is applied by hot-dipping or electroplating. Despite the name, a tin can contains only about 0.5% tin by weight — the bulk is steel. Aluminium cans for beverages are made entirely of aluminium, not steel.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Constantan is an alloy with a very stable electrical resistance across a wide temperature range. It is used in precision resistors and thermocouples. Its composition is approximately:
questions.explanation: Constantan is an alloy of approximately 55% copper (Cu) and 45% nickel (Ni). Its defining property is its near-zero temperature coefficient of electrical resistance — its resistance barely changes with temperature. This makes it ideal for precision resistors in instruments, strain gauges, and as the negative leg in Type T, J, and E thermocouples. It is also known as Eureka or Advance alloy.
questions.subject: chemistry

questions.stem: Sterling silver, the standard for silver jewellery and silverware worldwide, contains what proportion of actual silver?
questions.explanation: Sterling silver is 92.5% silver (Ag) and 7.5% copper (Cu), denoted as '925 silver.' Pure (fine) silver is too soft for everyday jewellery; the 7.5% copper adds hardness and durability. Sterling silver is hallmarked with '925' or a lion passant (in the UK). The term 'sterling' possibly derives from the Old Norman 'esterlin' meaning 'little star.' Brittania silver is 95.84% Ag (958 standard).
questions.subject: chemistry
